metas.name: Abbotsford  - White hydrant
metas.note: Abbotsford, British Columbia can be recognised by its white fire hydrants with a blue top and nozzles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Amherst  - Yellow body hydrant
metas.note:
While most cities in Nova Scotia use red body fire hydrants, there are some notable yellow exceptions. Amherst uses a yellow hydrant with a black nozzle and occasionally a black top.

Note: The town also has some fully yellow variants.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Barrie  - Downtown street sign
metas.note: Barrie is the most significant city in Simcoe county. The downtown area has some unique black street signs indicating the neighbourhood in a "Historic XY" format.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Barrie  - Street sign lines
metas.note:
Barrie is the most significant city in Simcoe county. Outside of a few downtown neighbourhoods Barrie uses a green street sign with a metal line on the top and the bottom.

Note: The downtown area has its own unique street sign which is black.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Brandon  - Blue bus stops
metas.note:
Brandon Manitoba has 2 kinds of bus stops:

  • a light blue rectangular sign commonly seen on Gen 3 coverage
  • a dark blue shark fin shape sign only seen on Gen 4 / main roads.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Brandon  - Rusted yellow hydrant
metas.note:
Brandon Manitoba uses these rusted yellow fire hydrants.

Note: Top and nozzle colours can vary.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Brandon  - Street sign clasps
metas.note: Brandon uses a green street sign with metal clasps which are different to Winnipeg's.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Brooklin  - Fancy roof ridge
metas.note: These designs on the end of roof ridges and dormers are extremely common in the town of Brooklin.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Burnaby  - "Clown" hydrant
metas.note: Burnaby, a satellite city just East of Vancouver uses a distinct colour scheme for its fire hydrants: a white body, red nozzles and a green top. Just like a clown's makeup!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Calgary  - Big trees
metas.note:
Calgary has a lot of big trees right up against people's homes.

Note: Obviously, Calgary won't be the only Canadian city where this happens.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Calgary  - Calgary Transit
metas.note: Calgary uses dark blue bus stops and red buses.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Calgary  - Neon hydrant
metas.note: Calgary fire hydrants are neon green with black nozzles. Very easy to spot!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Calgary  - No cap signpost
metas.note: Calgary's signposts have small casps and no cap. Edmonton's have small holes and a cap instead.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Calgary  - Yellow traffic light
metas.note: Calgary's traffic lights are fully yellow on both sides. Edmonton's are fully black on the front and Red Deer's are black in the middle with a yellow frame.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Cambridge Bay  - Landmark trekkers
metas.note:
Just accross the river from Cambridge Bay there are some interesting trekkers showing 3 landmarks. From North to South, these are:

  • A distinctly shaped monument to Roald Amundsen's polar ship "The Maud" with the actual shipwreck still in the bay
  • The Old Stone Church
  • Ruins of the Old Town.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Cambridge Bay  - Surrounding roads
metas.note:
Cambridge Bay has coverage on 2 roads surrounding the town:

  • the road to the Airport (West) has poles on the South/West side and snow poles on the other,
  • the road to the Cemetery (East) has water to the South/East.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Cambridge Bay  - Vibes
metas.note: Cambridge Bay coverage is wet, rainy and overcast. It is the only Gen 2 coverage in Nunavut, leaving this large pink blur in the sky - similar to Inuvik.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Carcross  - Vibes
metas.note: Carcross is surrounded by large mountains and water in all directions: Nares Lake to the East and Bennett Lake to the West. All coverage is cloudy Gen 2.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Carmacks  - Wooden street sign
metas.note: Carmacks has wooden street signs, just like Haines Junction. To identify Carmacks, look for the plain rectangular shape, the letters in italics and the brown signposts.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Carmacks  - Yellow lamp
metas.note:
You can identify the Klondike Highway going through Carmacks by the rusty yellow lamps.

Note: In true Yukon fashion, the lamps often have flags on them.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Carmacks  - Yukon River & hills
metas.note: Carmacks is located on the Yukon River and is surrounded by hills. While the town and the banks of the river has Gen 2 coverage only, the Klondike Highway and the Carmacks Bridge has Gen 4.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Charlottetown  - Asymmetrical poletop
metas.note:
Charlottetown uses a lot of asymmetrical poletops. They can have single or multiple insulator rods.

Note: Charlottetown also has some poletops that look similar to the ones used in Québec.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Charlottetown  - Horizontal traffic light
metas.note:
Prince Edward Island uses horizontal black traffic lights, just like Québec. This is only really applicable to Charlottetown.

Note: These diamond and square shaped lamps seem to be unique to PEI.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Charlottetown  - Red hydrant with green nozzles
metas.note:
Charlottetown uses red fire hydrants with a green top and green nozzles.

Note: On Gen 3 the nozzles are more generic grey.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Chilliwack  - Green-on-white street sign
metas.note: Chilliwack uses these unique green-on-white street signs. Also notice the metal sign clasps typical for South-Western B.C.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Churchill  - Antenna
metas.note:
The overcast Gen3 snow coverage in Churchill Manitoba can look similar to the Nunavut trekkers. Use the antenna on the right side on the car to recognise the town!

Note: The town has unique street signs.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Churchill Falls  - Halloween
metas.note:
Churchill Falls was covered around Halloween, so it is common to see Halloween decorations on people's homes.

Note: Churchill Falls is a scary town.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Churchill Falls  - Hills to the East
metas.note:
Churchill Falls can be recognised by its sunny Gen 4 coverage and two distinctive hills to the East.

Note: One is shaped like a lopsided pyramid, the other one has two bumps on top.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Churchill Falls  - Red hydrant with grey nozzle
metas.note: Churchill Falls has red body fire hydrants with a grey nozzle. It is commonly accompanied by a Québec-style hydrant marker of a yellow or red colour.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Churchill Falls  - Unique lamp
metas.note: This stylish lamp with a yellow sticker, standing on a concrete block is extremely common in Churchill Falls.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Corner Brook  - Hilliness
metas.note: Corner Brook is situated on a large hill and can be identified most of the time because of its hilliness.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Corner Brook  - Hydrant numbers
metas.note: Corner Brook marks all fire hydrants with numbers.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dauphin  - Black signpost
metas.note: Dauphin is a smaller town in Manitoba that follows all the same meta as Winnipeg: red fire hydrants, white street signs. The main difference is that Dauphin uses black sign posts for its street signs.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson City  - Airport Road
metas.note: This unique pole type runs from Dawson City to the Airport on the South side of the road. This combined with the foggy weather makes the road extremely easy to recognise.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson City  - Foggy mountains
metas.note: Dawson City is built in a valley. You will feel surrounded by epic mountains. A lot of the coverage is foggy, making the mountains barely visible.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Cmoprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson City  - Frontier-style architecture
metas.note: Dawson City's colourful frontier-style architecture makes the town look like a set for a Western movie.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson City  - July 2009
metas.note: The highlighted roads around Dawson City feature some unique July 2009 coverage. This coverage appears to be extremely dry and has a warm tinge to it. The birch trees will have a very bright white colour, similar to what is seen in Manitoba.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson City  - Unique street sign
metas.note: Dawson City uses uniquely shaped white street signs. Signposts are typically black or very rusted.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Dawson Creek  - "Smokey" with thin aspens
metas.note: The Dawson Creek region resembles Alberta with its flatness and its abundance of thin aspen trees. Older generation Dawson Creek coverage has a distinct "smokey feel" to it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Alleyway coverage
metas.note:
Edmonton has a lot of alleyway coverage.

Note: This type of coverage can be found in other large Canadian cities as well. Luckily, garbage bins with the city's logo and name are abundant in alleys.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Black traffic lights
metas.note:
Edmonton's traffic lights are fully black on the front and yellow on the back.

Note: Calgary's are yellow on both sides and Red Deer's are black in the middle with a yellow frame.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Blue nozzle hydrant
metas.note: Edmonton fire hydrants have a yellow body with a blue top and nozzles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Edmonton Transit System
metas.note:
Edmonton uses blue buses, blue bus stops and blue shelters.

Note: Sometimes you can see the ETS logo on them (Edmonton Transit System).
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Holey signpost
metas.note: Edmonton's signposts have small holes on the back and often have a cap on top. Calgary's have small casps and no cap.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Lamp sticker
metas.note: If you see a red sticker on the base of a lamp, it's 100% Edmonton. About half of the lamps have red, but you can also find it in white.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmonton  - Large base lamp
metas.note: In Edmonton many lamps have a large metal box for a base.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Edmundston  - Yellow hydrant with grey nozzle
metas.note:
Edmundston is the only major city in New Brunswick to use yellow fire hydrants. The nozzles are grey.

Note: Edmunston also uses Québec-style hydrant markers in various colours.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Enterprise  - Asymmetrical road lanes and bollards
metas.note: The best way to identify Enterprise is by the asymmetrical (2/1) road lanes. Apart from that, there are various bollards.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Estevan  - Yellow infrastructure
metas.note:
Estevan really likes the colour yellow. Yellow signposts, yellow fire hydrans, yellow curbs.

Note: Sadly, their lamps are green.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Faro  - Vibes
metas.note: Faro has limited and choppy Gen 4 coverage. It has a bright sunset with clear skies and a medium sized hill visible to the North. Faro also has some unique street signs indicating the town's name.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Flin Flon  - Brown street sign
metas.note: Flin Flon uses unique brown street signs. This is a very consistent clue.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Flin Flon  - Red-black hydrant
metas.note:
Flin Flon uses red fire hydrants with a black top and lots of yellow curbs.

Note: While none of these features are unique to Flin Flon, these together with the hazy Gen4 coverage is enough to identify the city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Flin Flon  - The Stack
metas.note: Flin Flon's iconic blue-grey chimney, "The Stack" is visible from far away. (Especially from the Western part of the city.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Frances  - Dark red hydrant
metas.note: Fort Frances features a dark red hydrant with a matching snow pole.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Frances  - Maple leaf street sign
metas.note: This fun looking maple leaf logo street sign is unique to Fort Frances. Note: They are only found downtown.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Liard  - Vibes
metas.note:
Fort Liard has only one road of coverage in town: Valley Main Street. It can be identified by:

  • the Québec-style curved lamps with a slight upward tilt and Québec-style connection pieces,
  • the yellow pole stickers,
  • the generic green street signs.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Mc Murray  - Blue street sign
metas.note: Fort Mc Murray is one of the only cities in Alberta that uses blue street signs. This is different from the rural ones which are almost always blue. Additionally, this street sign has no cardinal directions on it.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Mc Murray  - North white aspen trees
metas.note: Fort McMurray is easily identifiable from the north white aspen trees.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fort Mc Pherson  - Clear weather & long leg crates
metas.note:
Fort McPherson is a town located on the Dempster Highway. It looks a lot like Inuvik, but with clearer weather. Both towns have Gen 2 only.

Note: In Fort McPherson wooden garbage crates often have longer "legs" than in the other NWT towns.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Fort Simpson  - Vibes
metas.note:
Fort Simpson has one road of coverage: 100 St. South of the town this road will have guardrails with a lot of NWT bollards on them. Inside the town you will see Québec-style curved lamps and connection pieces, similar to the ones in Fort Liard.

Note: Fort Simpson has wider roads and looks more residential than Fort Liard.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fredericton  - Blue street sign
metas.note: Fredericton uses exclusively blue street signs. Most of New Brunswick uses green.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Fredericton  - Red hydrant with blue nozzle
metas.note: Fredericton uses red body fire hydrants with blue nozzles.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Gander  - White street sign with black text
metas.note: Gander uses white street signs, sometimes with bold black text.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Gander  - Yellow marker
metas.note: Gander uses a yellow pole to mark its fire hydrants instead of a diamond.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Gatineau  - Oval logo
metas.note: Gatineau's distinct oval logo shows up on street signs and garbage bins throughout the whole city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Granby  - Logo streetsign
metas.note: Granby uses this unique logo on street signs.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Cmoprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Granby  - STOP sign
metas.note: For some reason, the whole city of Granby uses "STOP" signs instead of the Québec "Arrêt". This might be the only place in Québec to do so.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Granby  - Yellow border hydrant marker
metas.note: Granby often uses a unique blue hydrant marker with a yellow border.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Grande Prairie  - Aquatera bin
metas.note: These grey garbage cans that say "Aquatera" are common and unique to Grande Prairie.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Grande Prairie  - Period street sign
metas.note: Grande Prairie always puts a period at the end of their street names.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Grande Prairie  - Yellow hydrant
metas.note: Grande Prairie is one of the only places in Alberta with yellow fire hydrants.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Grise Fjord  - Vibes
metas.note: Grise Fjord should be instantly recognisable by the unique mountains which are visible from all locs. Looking down, most of the time you can see the corner of a red quad bike. The trekker along the beach doesn't have the quad bike but the sea ice and the mountains give it away.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Haines Junction  - Mt. Martha Black
metas.note: The best way to identify Haines Junction is by the large mountain range to the Southwest called Mt. Martha Black. The town is also built on a hill: North is uphill, South is down. The range to the North is sometimes also visible, but much smaller.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Haines Junction  - Red and yellow hydrants
metas.note: Haines Junction fire hydrants can be red with yellow nozzles or fully yellow.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Haines Junction  - Street signs
metas.note:
Haines Junction's official street sign is made of wood. There are about 10 of these in the town, the rest of the signs are green with a white border, standard in Yukon.

Note: Carmacks also has wooden street signs, but they are more rectangular and never have green signposts.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Halifax  - Fake Québec poletop
metas.note:
Halifax has a lot of these "Québec-like" poletops. Within Nova Scotia, this is mostly a Halifax thing.

Note: This poletop shows up in various places within Atlantic Canada, including NS. Only go Halifax if see a lot of it and you feel like you are in a big enough city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Halifax  - Flat lamp
metas.note: Lamps in Halifax have a distinct flat shape.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Halifax  - Halifax Transit
metas.note: Halifax Transit has a distinct white-blue-yellow colour scheme that appears on buses and bus stops as well. Their designs often involve the letter "X" - or at least a part of it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Halifax  - Orange hydrant
metas.note: Halifax uses unique orange fire hydrants. Dartmouth, on the opposite side of the Bedford Basin uses the standard red hydrants of Nova Scotia.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Halifax  - Tufts Cove smokestacks
metas.note: The smokestacks of the Tufts Cove Generating Station are an integral part of the Halifax skyline. The station is located in the neighbouring Dartmouth and has 3 tall chimneys with red and white stripes that can be spotted from far away.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Hamilton  - Attached stop sign
metas.note: Stop signs in Hamilton are often attached perpendicular to a sign or post, this is rare in Ontario.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Hamilton  - Blue Area strip
metas.note: Speed signs in Hamilton often have a blue "area" strip. This can be occasionally found elsewhere in Ontario, but are especially common in Hamilton.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Happy Valley - Architecture
metas.note: Architecture in Happy Valley-Goose Bay is characterised by light coloured buildings with generally flat roofs.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Happy Valley - Coverage
metas.note:
Happy Valley-Goose Bay can be identified by its:

  • gloomy November Gen 4 coverage
  • relative flatness with blue ridges in the distance
  • being larger than any other town in Labrador
  • extreme sandiness.

Note: North West River looks similar, but way hillier.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Happy Valley - Hydrant variants
metas.note:
The classic Happy Valley-Goose Bay fire hydrant is red with a yellow top and blue nozzles. A more modest-looking red variant is also common there.

Note: The rainbow coloured ones usually come with a little red-white flag as a marker.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Happy Valley - Short lamp
metas.note: Happy Valley-Goose Bay uses a very short style of lamp.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Inner Vancouver  - Red hydrant
metas.note:
The City of Vancouver proper uses uniform red fire hydrants.

Note: Satellite cities such as Surrey, Burnaby, or North Vancouver use different colours.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Inukjuak  - Vibes
metas.note:
Inukjuak is a town on the coast of the Hudson Bay in Northern Québec. It can be recognised by the snowmobile coverage with the distinct rearview mirrors and the blurred driver.

Sanikiuaq looks similar, but there you can see a driver wearing a brown coat.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + Plonkit.net

metas.name: Inuvik  - Garbage crates
metas.note: In Inuvik, large wooden or metal garbage crates can be found at the end of many driveways. They are similar to what you see in Yellowknife.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Inuvik  - Pink Gen 2 blur
metas.note: Inuvik shows up a lot on the default Canada map because of its northernliness. You can recognise it by its gloomy weather and the extremely pink Gen 2 blur on the sky.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Inuvik  - Yellow guardrail & bollard
metas.note: The Northern town of Inuvik boasts some unique yellow guardrails and a yellow bollard.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Iqaluit  - Fortified hydrant
metas.note:
Fire hydrants in Iqualuit are quite unique: they are "fortified" by 3-4 thick red bollards and a triangular marker.

Note: Sometimes the bollards don't have a hydrant in the middle.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Iqaluit / Apex  - Bilingual signs
metas.note: In Iqualuit and Apex street signs, stop signs and pretty much everything else is bilingual in the Inuktitut and English languages.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Iqaluit / Apex  - Road to Apex
metas.note: The road between Iqaluit and Apex can be identified by the bollards and the poles. It's also worth mentioning that Iqaluit is a trekker, so the camera is on the side of the road, not the middle.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kamloops  - 2 bolts street sign
metas.note:
Kamloops uses this unique green street sign with two bolts on the left side.

Note: Kelowna street signs are blue with no bolts.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kamloops  - White top hydrant
metas.note:
Fire hydrants in Kamloops are yellow with a white top and nozzles. This distinguishes them from Kelowna hydrants which use different top colours.

Tip: In general, cities between Prince George and the US border will have yellow hydrants, while Eastern and Western BC uses red.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kangiqsuallujuaq  - Vibes
metas.note:
Kangiqsuallujuaq is a town in far Northern Québec. It can be identified by the green rocky hills surrounding it, with trees visible in the distance.

Note: I think the hills give a vaguely North-European vibe.
metas.footer: meta from: Plonkit.net

metas.name: Kelowna  - Fruit plantations
metas.note: The Okanagan Valley is very distinct. It has a semi-arid climate and can look almost mediterranean. In and around Kelowna fruit plantations (orchards, vinyards) are a common sight.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kelowna  - Green bus stop
metas.note: Kelowna has a lot of green bus stops and a blue street sign with white letters. The street sign can have a few variations.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kelowna  - Yellow hydrant
metas.note:
While the classic Kelowna fire hydrant is yellow with a blue top, other colour variations exist in the city. The most common variant has an orange top and nozzles.

Tip: In general, cities between Prince George and the US border will have yellow hydrants, while Eastern and Western BC uses red.
metas.footer: meta from: Street View find.

metas.name: Kenora  - "Manitoba" dirt
metas.note: In Kenora the dirt has a similar light colour to what you would find in Manitoba. Note: This dirt is often visible on the pavement too.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kenora  - Exposed rocks
metas.note: Kenora is quite hilly and has exposed rocks even on residential streets.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kenora  - Yellow hydrant with red pole
metas.note: Kenora fire hydrants are yellow and always have a red snow pole attached.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kingston  - Black lamps
metas.note: Downtown Kingston (mainly Princess St. and Queen St.) has unique black traffic lights and lamps.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kingston  - White pole sticker
metas.note: In Kingston lamps and utility poles are tagged with a white sticker with numbers on it. This is a consistent meta.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kingston  - White sticker hydrant
metas.note: Kingston has a white sticker with the letter "H" followed by numbers on its fire hydrants. This is a very consistent meta.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kitchener  - Extra thicc sign border
metas.note: Twin cities Kitchener and Waterloo both use these extra thick white outline sign borders. Note: Kitchener mostly uses blue while Waterloo prefers green.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Kitchener / Waterloo  - Arched bus stop
metas.note: Twin cities Kitchener and Waterloo feature bus stops with a uniquely arched shape.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Labrador City  - Northwest hills and poletop
metas.note: Labrador City has only one road of coverage. This road can be recognised by the hills to the Northwest and the tall wooden poles with a trident poletop.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Lake Ontario area  - Red body hydrant
metas.note:
The West Coast of Lake Ontario (the regions of Hamilton, Halton, Peel and Niagara Falls) most commonly uses red body hydrants. Generally, the rest of Ontario uses a yellow body.

Note: St. Catharines uses the usual Ontario yellows.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Lethbridge  - Street sign layout
metas.note:
Lethbridge uses the street number - kind of street - cardinal direction format for its street signs.

Note: Calgary and Medicine hat uses block capital letters for the kind of street. Lethbridge only capitalizes the first letter.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: London  - Black number sticker
metas.note: This unique black sticker is found on almost every pole in London. They can start with a letter (mostly "SW", "T" or "P") or just feature 5 numbers without any letter.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: London  - LT Symbol
metas.note: The London Transit Commission has a recognisable "LT" symbol.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: London  - Yellow hydrant with blue nozzle
metas.note: London's hydrants will almost always have blue nozzles.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Mayo  - Vibes
metas.note:
Mayo can be recognised by a large forested hill to the South, the wooden street signs and the fully red fire hydrants marked by 3 red bollards. The town has a mix of Gen 2 and Gen 4 coverage.

Note: Wooden street signs can be found in multiple towns in the Yukon (eg. Haines Junction or Carmacks).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Medicine Hat  - Bicolour traffic light
metas.note: Medicine Hat has some really stylish traffic lights with a yellow-black-yellow pattern. These are unique to the city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Medicine Hat  - Connection piece
metas.note: Street signs in Medicine Hat often have metal connection pieces between the sign and the post. They can be T-shape or U-shape.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Medicine Hat  - Dry ridges
metas.note: Medicine has a distinctively dry landscape with many dry ridges in and around the city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Medicine Hat  - Green lamp
metas.note:
Medicine Hat uses a lot of green lamps. Surrounding cities often use brown.

Note: In some neighbourhoods the lamps can appear rusty.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Medicine Hat / Lethbridge  - Red body hydrant
metas.note: Medicine Hat uses red body fire hydrants along with Lethbridge. While Medicine Hat uses white nozzles, Lethbridge uses black.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moncton  - Bell Aliant Tower
metas.note: The huge white Bell Aliant Tower is visible from most of Downtown Moncton. (Where you see blue street signs you will probably also see the tower.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moncton  - Downtown logo
metas.note: Downtown Moncton uses a blue street sign with a city logo. The rest of the city uses the standard green signs with white lettering.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Moncton  - Horizontal traffic light
metas.note: Moncton uses a horizontal traffic light with a black middle and a yellow frame. This is rare in New Brunswick.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moncton  - Red snow pole hydrant
metas.note: Moncton always has a red snowpole besides its fire hydrants.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Black signback
metas.note: Montréal's inner city tends to use black backs of signs, lamps, signposts and other inftrastructure. Note: Other colours are possible.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Brown compost bin
metas.note: These small brown compost bins are specific to Montréal. Note: Even if you can't see the city name on the front, you can recognise the bin by its colour and the unique trash circle logo.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Chevron bus
metas.note: Montréal's buses have pretty distinctive "chevrons".
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Flower logo
metas.note: Montréal is easily identifiable thanks to the red flower logo on nearly all street signs. Street sign logos are a great way to identify cities in Québec.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Red hydrant with yellow marker
metas.note: Red fire hydrants with yellow snowpoles are typical for Montréal.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Montréal  - Vertical stoplight
metas.note: Downtown Montréal sometimes uses vertical stoplights which is an exception to the standard Québec style.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moose Jaw  - Green wooden lamppost
metas.note: Moose Jaw uses green painted wood for its lampposts. In some streets the paint can be quite faded.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moose Jaw  - MJTS bus stop
metas.note: Moose Jaw uses orange bus stop signs with an MJTS label.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Moose Jaw  - Silver nozzles
metas.note: Fire hydrants in Moose Jaw are red with a silver top and silver nozzles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Mount Pearl  - Red-green hydrant
metas.note: Mount Pearl, just Southwest of St. John's has its own red fire hydrant design with a green top and nozzles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Mount Pearl / Torbay  - Arched street sign
metas.note: Mount Pearl and Torbay are both part of the St. John's Metropolitan area. They have similar metas to St. John's, except for their unique blue arched street signs. To tell them apart, you can look at what's inside the arch: Torbay has a logo with a bird and a wave and Mount Pearl has a crest surrounded by a "City of Mount Pearl" text.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Nain  - Trekker coverage
metas.note:
Nain is the northernmost town with coverage in Labrador. It was covered by a trekker during some sort of an event. There are often groups of people walking around the camera.

Note: The pine trees and the rocky cliffs on the other side of the bay are also distinctive.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + Plonkit.net

metas.name: Nanaimo  - White outline
metas.note:
The city of Nanaimo (which is on Vancouver Island) uses a thick white outline on a blue street sign + yellow curbs.

Note: This street sign is "T" shape as opposed to Victoria's "L" shape ones.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Nelson  - Green signpost
metas.note: The city of Nelson uses distinct green signposts.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Nelson  - Post-rain May
metas.note:
The typical coverage in Nelson has a humid, post-rain look with gray clouds and lush, vegetation covered mountains all around. The photos were taken in May 2025 with a Gen4 camera.

Note: The old Gen3 September coverage still exists, but it's mostly limited to the surrounding forest roads.
metas.footer: meta from: Street View find.

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Vertical traffic light
metas.note:
The standard Newfoundland & Labrador traffic light is vertical, yellow and has no frame. (This is only applicable to bigger towns.)

Note: The town of Gander is an exception with its black lights.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Niagara Falls  - Blue Transit
metas.note: Niagara Falls uses blue bus stop signs and buses that are either fully white or white with a wave pattern on the front.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Niagara Falls  - Fire route numbers
metas.note: Niagara Falls sometimes has fire route numbers on its street signs.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Niagara Falls  - Octagonal lamppost
metas.note:
Suburban lampposts in Niagara Falls often use an octagonal concrete design.

Note: Lampposts are usually tagged with a yellow horizontal plate with numbers on it in a XX-XXX format.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Nort West River / Sheshatshiu  - Landscape
metas.note: North West River and Sheshatshiu are found just North of Happy Valley. They look similar to Happy Valley, only hillier and located on a river.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: North West River  - Anniversary street sign
metas.note: North West River has its own street sign with an anniversary logo inside a semicircle on the top.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Okanagan Valley  - Dryness
metas.note:
Kamloops, Kelowna and the whole Okanagan Valley is very dry, which looks pretty different to the rest of Canada. This region is very distinct and can look almost Mediterranean. Winyards and fruit plantations are a common sight here.

Note: Kamloops is located in the transition zone between the Okanagan and the wetter North so it can look somewhat greener than Kelowna.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa  - Bent metal signpost
metas.note:
Ottawa signposts often use a single piece of bent metal, whereas the rest of Ontario prefers these dotted square signposts shown on the second image.

Note: Be careful, bent metal signposts can also have holes on them!
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa  - Bilingual signage
metas.note: Ottawa will almost always have bilingual signage due to its proximity and relation with Québec.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa  - Blue cap hydrant
metas.note: Fire hydrants in Ottawa have a distinct blue cap on top, but are still the standard Ontario yellow.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa  - Bus stop
metas.note: Ottawa's bus stop can be recognised by the red quarter "O" symbol in the top right corner.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa  - Circular city logo
metas.note:
The Ottawa street sign can be recognised by the circular logo and the bilingualism. Blue street signs are rare in Ontario, most rural areas use green.

Note: Downtown Ottawa has some unique colour variantions, but the logo stays the same.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ottawa / Gatineau  - Car plate chaos
metas.note:
Because Ottawa is a connected city with Gatineau, main roads in these 2 cities will often have a mix of Ontario and Québec car plates. Only Ontario requires front plates.

Note: This is less common in residential areas.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: PEI  - Conferederation Bridge
metas.note: This huge bridge with a lump in the middle is the Confederation Bridge connecting Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Pelly Crossing  - Vibes
metas.note: Pelly Crossing is a town located on the Klondike Highway. It has only highway coverage, mostly Gen 4 with the light blue Pelly River Bridge always in sight. Northern Tutchone, the traditional language of the Selkirk First Nation is featured on the street signs.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prince Albert  - Green signpost
metas.note:
Street sign posts in Prince Albert are often green.

Note: Their other common signpost is a thick, white wooden one which is used for holding street signs as well as traffic signs. You will often see both kind in the same intersecion.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prince Albert  - Red hydrant
metas.note:
Fire hydrants in Prince Albert are red.

Note: On the older Gen 3 coverage hydrants often had a blue top, but these have been faded or replaced by the time the Gen 4 photos were taken.
metas.footer: meta from: Street View find.

metas.name: Prince Albert  - Thick white signpost
metas.note:
Thick white wooden signposts are characteristic of Prince Albert.

Note: Thin green plastic signposts are also common there.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prince George  - Green lamp
metas.note: Prince George likes to use green lamps.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prince George  - Yellow hydrant
metas.note: Just like most cities in Central BC, Prince George uses fire hydrants with a yellow body. The top and the nozzles are usually red, but plain yellow hydrants are also fairly common.
metas.footer: Meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Qikiqtarjuak  - Vibes
metas.note:
Qikiqtarjuak is very mountainous. Other than Grise Fjord, it is the only town in Nunavut with mountains this large. Its reddish dirt is also distinct.

Note: The hazy Gen 3 with the red dirt makes this town very vibeable.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec City  - Blue rectangle
metas.note: All hydrant markers in Québec City will use this blue rectangle on the side. This is a very reliable meta.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec City  - European architecture
metas.note: The downtown part of Québec City is a tourist attraction because of its European architecture.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec City  - RTC Buses
metas.note: Public transit in Québec City is operated by RTC (Reseau du Transport de la Capitale). Their buses are either lime green or dark blue, with a wide grey diagonal strip on the side.
metas.footer: meta from: Street View find.

metas.name: Québec City  - Street sign layout
metas.note: No logo on the street sign for Québec City, but the white background, the black text and the layout is memorable. Note: Many of these street signs will have a tiny font size for the kind of street (Rue, Avenue, etc.) and the cardinal directions and a much bigger font for the street name.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Red Bay  - Vibes
metas.note:
Red Bay is a coastal town in Southern Labrador. It looks a bit like Nain, but the soil is redder and most of the houses are painted white. The weather is also gloomier.

Note: The lack of huge pine trees typical of Nain is also noteworthy.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Red Deer  - Dark lamp
metas.note: Lamps painted dark are common in Red Deer. Neither Edmonton nor Calgary uses dark lamps.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Red Deer  - Lime green hydrant
metas.note:
Red Deer has lime green fire hydrants with a row of numbers on top.

Note: While Calgary's hydrants have a similar green body, their nozzles are black.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Red Deer  - Metal connection
metas.note: Red Deer has a lot of numbered streets and their street signs emphasize the numbers. The signs are usually connected horizontally with a small piece of metal on the pole side, but signs connected from below are also common.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensice Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Red Deer  - Traffic light
metas.note:
Red Deer uses traffic lights with black lamps inside of a yellow frame. Edmonton's lights are fully black in the front and Calgary's are fully yellow.

Note: Red Deer is half way between Edmonton and Calgary - and so is the traffic light's colouring!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Red Deer  - Yellow curbs
metas.note:
Yellow painted curbs and sewers are especially common in Red Deer, along with many rural Alberta towns.

Note: Yellow curbs show up in other parts of Canada too, so look for other clues first!
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Regina  - Blue street sign
metas.note: Regina is the only major city in Saskatchewan with blue street signs.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Regina  - Horizontal street light
metas.note:
Traffic lights in Regina are fully yellow and horizontal. Saskatoon's are vertical.

Note: Horizontal traffic lights are not unique to Regina, they are pretty standard in Sask.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Regina  - Regina Transit
metas.note: Regina Transit has a useful colour scheme: the blue and yellow stripes are visible on their buses and their bus stops as well.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Regina  - Small holes signpost
metas.note: Regina and Saskatoon signposts are both rectangular with no holes. However, the lowest section on Regina's posts does feature some small holes. You can use this to differentiate between the two cities.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Resolute  - Road to Airport
metas.note: The road to Resolute Bay Airport has a row of snow poles on the West side. A bit further behind them there is also a row of generic utility poles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Resolute  - Vibes
metas.note: Resolute can be recognised by the cloudy skies and the small ridge to the North with patchy snow. It feels like a less mountainous version of Qikiqtarjuak with Kyrgyzstan vibes.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ross River  - Vibes
metas.note:
Ross River has cloudy Gen 2 coverage with a distinct ridge to the North. Its street signs are the standard Yukon green with a white border. Yield signs are common in the town.

The gravel road leading into the town from the West has sunny Gen 4 coverage.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saguenay  - City logo
metas.note: Saguenay's city logo shows up on street signs and garbage bins in the city. The colour scheme is blue-white. Note: A simpler green sign with white letters and no logo is also possible to find.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage (plus some original research).

metas.name: Saguenay  - Red hydrant, red marker
metas.note: Saguenay's hydrant markers match their hydrant's red colour. Some suburbs use this unique sketch-like drawing instead.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saint John  - Dark signpost
metas.note: Signposts in Saint John are often extremely rusty or dark.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saint John  - European vibe
metas.note: Downtown Saint John has a very unique European vibe.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saint John  - Grey nozzle hydrant
metas.note: Saint John uses red fire hydrants with a grey nozzle.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saint John  - Hills
metas.note: Saint John is hillier than other major cities in New Brunswick.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saint John  - Saint John Transit
metas.note: Saint John buses are white with a red and blue pattern on the front. Bus stops are orange and black.
metas.footer: metas from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Sanikiluaq  - Vibes
metas.note: Coverage in Sanikiluaq can be identified by the snowmobiler wearing a dark brown coat. Sanikiluaq is easily confused with Inukjuak, a town in Northern Québec which has similar snowmobile coverage, but without the brown coat.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sarnia  - Orange bus stop
metas.note: Sarnia's bus stops are very noticeably orange. They can be seen from far away.
metas.footer: meta source: original find.

metas.name: Saskatoon  - Green street sign
metas.note: Saskatoon uses the standard green street signs with white lettering. Regina uses blue.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatoon  - Red top hydrant
metas.note: Saskatoon and Regina both use yellow body fire hydrants, however only Saskatoon has red tops on them.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatoon  - Saskatoon Transit
metas.note: Saskatoon Transit uses distinct blue shark-fin shaped bus stops and buses with a sky blue front.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatoon  - Vertical street light
metas.note: Saskatoon and Regina both use yellow traffic lights, but only Saskatoon's is vertical. This is quite rare in Saskatchewan.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - Black middle street light
metas.note: Street lights in Sault Ste. Marie are black in the middle.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - Red hydrant with blue top
metas.note: Sault Ste. Marie is one of the few cities in Ontario that use red fire hydrants. Below is the unique hydrant style with a blue top.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sault Ste. Marie  - White stripe street sign
metas.note: Sault Ste. Marie uses these unique blue street signs with white or metallic strips on the top and bottom.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sherbrooke  - Blue or green dot
metas.note: Sherbrooke's hydrant markers often have a blue or green dot inside one of the small rectangles. Otherwise they are pretty standard for Québec.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sherbrooke  - No Q pole sticker
metas.note: Sherbrooke and surrounding cities use a pole sticker without the usual Québec "black Q". The sticker will only have the vertical numbers and possibly some other letters on top.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sherbrooke  - Plain blue street sign
metas.note: Sherbrooke uses these minimalistic looking blue street signs. Note: On the 2011 coverage you might see their old green sign with a Sherbrooke logo. This coverage is extremely rare these days, so I wouldn't worry about it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sherbrooke  - Wavy bin logo
metas.note: Sherbrooke garbage bins come with this very convenient city logo featuring the city's name riding a wave.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Southwest BC Cities  - Sign clasps
metas.note:
Towns in South-West B.C. use thick metal sign clasps to attach their signs to the signpost.

Note: This includes the Vancouver Metro Area, Victoria and towns on the Sea-to-Sky Highway. For some reason, Nanaimo doesn't use them.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: St. John's  - Colourful houses
metas.note: St. John's is by far the largest city in Newfoundland & Labrador. The downtown area has many colourful houses.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: St. John's  - Torbay's arched street sign
metas.note: Mount Pearl and Torbay are both part of the St. John's Metropolitan area. They have similar metas to St. John's, except for their unique blue arched street signs. To tell them apart, you can look at what's inside the arch: Torbay has a logo with a bird and a wave and Mount Pearl has a crest surrounded by a "City of Mount Pearl" text.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: St. John's  - Yellow hydrant and diamond
metas.note:
Within Newfoundland, yellow fire hydrants and these skinny diamond snowpoles are unique to St. John's.

Note: The colour of the diamond may vary.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sudbury  - Mineral rocks
metas.note: Sudbury is a major mining hub located near the Sudbury Basin: an ancient meteorite impact crater. As a result, roads in the city are lined with walls of mineral-rich rocks. They look sharper and more colourful than the Canadian Shield protrusions found in other cities.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Sudbury  - Standard street sign
metas.note:
Sudbury uses the Ontario standard from almost everything: metal signposts (Thunder bay uses wood), green street signs and yellow fire hydrants.

Note: While the hydrants are mostly pure yellow, dark coloured tops can also be found in the city.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sudbury  - Transit logos
metas.note: Sudbury has a variety of bus stop designs: one features a bus icon and the Sudbury logo, the other says "gova" in colourful letters. The buses are white and also have the "gova" logo.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Sudbury  - Yellow pole marking
metas.note: Sudbury uses THICK yellow utility pole markings. They will always start with an "S" in Sudbury.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sudbury / Thunder Bay  - "Atlantic" sytle architecture
metas.note:
The architecture in Thunder Bay and Sudbury is different from Southern Ontario's. It resembles Atlantic Canada with more white siding material.

Note: Northern Ontario towns, such Kenora have similar architecture.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Summerside  - Pole star
metas.note: Summerside has some pretty unique stars between the wires.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Summerside  - Unique street sign
metas.note:
Summerside has unique blue street signs with a logo inside a semicircle and the town's name written underneath. The text is usually bilingual, which is less common in Charlottetown.

Note: The sign is often hanging from an ornate attachment piece.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Summerside  - White nozzle hydrant
metas.note: Summerside uses red hydrants with a white nozzle, accompanied by a red snow pole. Charlottetown uses green or grey nozzles and no snowpole.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Summerside  - Yellow pole sticker
metas.note:
Summerside always uses these yellow pole stickers, just like New Brunswick. The rest of Prince Edward Island uses the white horizontal sticker.

Note: The sticker often starts with an "S" in Summerside.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Swift Current  - Black traffic light
metas.note:
Swift Current uses fully black traffic lights.

Note: Black traffic lights show up in Moose Jaw and occasionally in Estevan too. We could say it's a Southern Sask thing.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Swift Current  - Blue nozzle hydrant
metas.note: Swift Current used to have a lot of red hydrants with a blue nozzle on the older Gen 3 coverage. On Gen 4, the nozzles can be other dark colours too, such as dark green or grey.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Sydney  - "Western style" traffic light
metas.note:
Sydney uses a vertical yellow traffic light with a yellow frame which is common in Nova Scotia. Within Atlantic Canada, this design indicates NS.

Note 1: Some Western provinces (BC, SK, MB) use the same design, but the landscape is usually enough to tell them apart.

Note 2: If you see thin horizontal slots on the frame: those are specific to Nova Scotia.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Sydney  - Secondary crossbeam
metas.note: Sydney and other major cities in Nova Scotia sometimes use secondary crossbeams.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Sydney  - Transit Cape Breton
metas.note:
Sydney is the largest settlement on Cape Breton Island. The city's transit system is part of Transit Cape Breton whose name you will see on the city's buses. Bus stops say "CBRM - Cape Breton Regional Municipality".

Note: Even if you can't read the text, the green colour scheme is a good clue.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Teslin  - Vibes
metas.note: Teslin is a town along the Alaska Highway. It has Gen 2 coverage only and a distinct hill to the Northwest. All lamps in Teslin have the same 2 flags.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thompson  - Overcast Gen2
metas.note: Thompson is basically the northernmost major town in Manitoba. It has only overcast Gen2 coverage with a red tinted halo in the sky.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thompson  - Pointy lamp
metas.note: Thompson uses a lot of this green lamp with a pointy top which is unique to Manitoba.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thunder Bay  - Bus stop
metas.note:
Thunder Bay bus stops can be identified by a bus icon inside a lime green circle.

Note: The sign also features the 807 area code.
metas.footer: meta from: looking around on Street View.

metas.name: Thunder Bay  - Light yellow hydrants
metas.note:
Thunder Bay fire hydrants tend to be a lighter shade of yellow than the normal Ontario ones. The nozzles are also fully yellow, whereas most of Southern Ontario has coloured nozzles.

Note: Snow poles are optional.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thunder Bay  - Metal strip street sign
metas.note:
Street signs in Thunder Bay have a distinct design with a small strip of metal at the bottom with 2 screws. The post is square and wooden and has a recognisable shape.

Note: The metal strip can also be on the side of the sign.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thunder Bay  - Poor quality pavement
metas.note: To tell Thunder Bay apart from Sudbury: Thunder Bay is economically poorer and experiences cold Winters. As a result, cracks, potholes and tar snakes can often be seen on the pavement.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Thunder Bay  - Ridge to the South
metas.note:
This large, distinct mountain is found to the South in Thunder Bay. It is the best way to recognise this city and is visible from many angles.

Note: The mountain might not be visible from the Northern half of the city.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Timmins  - Number street sign
metas.note: On Timmins street signs you can see house numbers diplayed vertically on the two sides of the street name.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - CN Tower
metas.note: The CN Tower is the main landmark of Toronto and can be seen from surprisingly far away. Note: This is mostly true for the Downtown areas and Centre Island.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - Coloured nozzles
metas.note: Toronto uses the standard Ontario yellow hydrant. Sometimes it uses coloured nozzles to indicate water flow. (Often blue).
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - Downtown Toronto lamp
metas.note: This lamp is specific to downtown Toronto.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - Garbage bin logo
metas.note: Most garbage bins in Toronto have a recognisable Toronto logo on them.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - Stripy street sign
metas.note: Within Toronto most street signs follow this unique stripy design. Note: The blue-white design has some interesting variations.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Toronto  - Transit logo
metas.note:
Toronto Transit Commission (TTC) has a unique red logo that can be seen on bus and subway stops.

Note: The bus stop signs themselves are thin and have the same red and white colour scheme.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Trois Riviéres  - Extra small hydrant marker
metas.note: Trois-Rivières uses an extra small yellow square to mark hydrants.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Trois Riviéres  - White border street sign
metas.note: Trois-Rivières uses a green street sign with a thick white border.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Tulita  - Vibes
metas.note: The brown dirt, the overcast skies and the short trees make Tulita easily recognisable. Sometimes you will see a white Google car with a bumper and an antenna on the right side. Sometimes only the antenna will be visible. For NMPZ: The main street has a unique poletop with 6 tiny insulators and a super short lamp.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Val - 'd Or - Ordinal numbers
metas.note: Val-'d Or street signs can be green or white, but the layout of the ordinal numbers is pretty distinct.
metas.footer: meta source: Street View find.

metas.name: Val - 'd Or - Red-blue hydrant
metas.note: Val-'d Or uses these neat red fire hydrants with blue nozzles and a blue top.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Vancouver  - Bus design
metas.note: Vancouver has a recognisable bus design: it's blue in the front and silver in the back.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Vancouver area  - Common design hydrant
metas.note:
The most common fire hydrant design in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area features a red body and white nozzles.

Note: Vancouver City uses red nozzles and Burnaby has its own colour scheme.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Vancouver Island  - Tall dense trees
metas.note:
Trees on Vancouver Island - including urban areas like Victoria and Nanaimo - are taller and denser. Parts of the island are a temperate rainforest.

Note: Giant hemlock trees are especially common here.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Vancouver Island  - Yellow curbs
metas.note:
Vancouver Island likes to use more yellow curbs than Vancouver City.

Note: Be careful, yellow curbs can be found in other areas of Canada!
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Victoria  - "L" street sign
metas.note: Street signs in Victoria are mostly in an "L" shape.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Victoria  - Green transit design
metas.note: Buses in Victoria have green stripes compared to Vancouver buses which have blue bottoms. Victoria also uses green stops, which can be either a regular square sign or a unique vertical design.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Victoria  - White logo sign
metas.note:
The Township of Esquimalt, just West of Victoria uses its own street sign with the city's logo on it. This is not an "L" shape sign, like Victoria's.

Note: On the 2025 coverage the logo can be completely faded.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Wabush  - Rain and street sign
metas.note:
Wabush, a town just South of Labrador City has only one road of coverage. This road can be identified by the rainy weather and the street signs with a red text.

Note: The clouds and the Sun being low on the horizon makes this coverage distinctly dark.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Watson Lake  - Blue green lamp
metas.note: All Watson Lake locations on the Alaska Highway can be identified by these blue-green lamps. The lamps lining the main road are decorated with several flags.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Cmoprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Watson Lake  - Sign Post Forest
metas.note: Watson Lake's "Sign Post Forest" is one of the most well-known landmarks along the Alaska Highway. It is situated at the intersection of the Alaska and the Robert Campbell Highways and is visible from the highlighted sections.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Western BC towns  - Cloudy mountains
metas.note:
The Western cities are almost always identifiable due to their very cloudy, gray and mountainous coverage.

Note: While the weather conditions are more striking in Gen2, the clouds are visible on Gen4 as well.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Asymmetrical poletop
metas.note:
This poletop with an asymmetrical secondary crossbeam is especially common in and around Whitehorse.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Bin logo
metas.note:
The official logo of the City of Whitehorse can be found on the garbage bins. It features a steamboat with the city's name underneath.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Number hydrant
metas.note:
The typical Whitehorse fire hydrant is yellow and features black numbers on the front part.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Rocky ridges
metas.note:
Whitehorse is surrounded by large, sandy, light coloured ridges.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Rusted or replaced lamps
metas.note:
Lamps in Whitehorse are rusted, giving it a brown colour. Some neighbourhoods have freshly painted yellow or silver lamps.

Note: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Whitehorse  - Steamboat street sign
metas.note:
Street signs in Whitehorse are green and have a distinct steamboat logo on it, with "Whitehorse" written underneath.

Note 1: On the older Gen 2 coverage a white street sign with a green border can be seen instead. Note 2: All Gen 4 coverage in Whitehorse has a foggy blur on the front left side of the camera.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Windsor  - Yellow hydrant with blue top
metas.note: Most of the fire hydrants in Windsor are yellow with a blue top.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - Go thru sign attachment
metas.note:
This type of sign attachment is unique to Winnipeg.

Note: 2 metal pieces pass through the sign from behind, so you can see 2 bolts on the front.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - Manitoba traffic light
metas.note: Winnipeg uses vertical yellow traffic lights. These are pretty standard for Manitoba. To differentiate between Manitoba and Ontario traffic lights, look at the top lamp: in Ontario it is bigger than the rest, in Manitoba it is the same size.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - Orange snow pole
metas.note:
Winnipeg usually has an orange snow pole beside the fire hydrant.

Note: Exceptions do exist.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - White pole sticker
metas.note:
Winnipeg uses large, white pole stickers with black numbers on some of its utility poles.

Note: These stickers are somewhat common in alleyways, but extremely rare elsewhere.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - White street sign
metas.note: Winnipeg street signs are always white.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Winnipeg  - Winnipeg Transit
metas.note: Winnipeg buses are white with thin blue, yellow and red stripes on their side. Bus stops feature the "T" transit logo, in front of 3 diagonal stripes.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Yarmouth  - Yellow body hydrant
metas.note: While most cities in Nova Scotia use red body fire hydrants, there are some notable yellow exceptions. Yarmouth has a yellow body hydrant with various top colours.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Yellowknife  - Garbage bin
metas.note: Large wooden garbage bins of this specific shape are found in many driveways in Yellowknife. They can be painted in different colours.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Yellowknife  - Green lamp
metas.note:
Green lamps are the main characteristic feature of Yellowknife. Whitehorse uses dark brown lamps.

Note: Yellowknife is Gen 2 only.
metas.footer: meta and text from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.
